extracted.intended_audience: general readers of literary biography and readers interested in Elias Hicks / Quaker history
extracted.subtask_description: A literary biographical-essay sketch of a historical/religious figure (Elias Hicks) that blends life chronology with reflections on doctrine, oratory, and character. Focus is on conveying personality, preaching style, and moral/philosophical outlook through anecdote and quotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious missionary life (qualities)
rubrics_metrics.description: His whole life was a long religious missionary life of method, practicality, sincerity, earnestness, and pure piety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page treats a successful missionary life as sustained, methodical, practical, sincere and earnest. Evidence includes hundreds of preaching visits over decades, long itineraries (thousands of miles), frequent meetings attended, and persistence into old age. The characterization is supported by summaries of travel logs (durations, mileage, number of meetings) and by the subject's quotidian discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Itinerant-ministry practice (financial conduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: He scrupulously accepted in payment only his transportation from place to place, with his own food and shelter, and never received a dollar of money for 'salary' or preaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a standard of evangelical/pietistic integrity: travel widely to minister, but refuse monetary salary; accept only necessary expenses. The text uses this as a mark of humility and probity, noting that he continued such practice throughout his long ministry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oratory style: natural, extempore, magnetic
rubrics_metrics.description: Not argumentative or intellectual, but penetrating—unstudied oratory emanating from the heart; extempore, often mystical and radical, producing deep emotional response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualities include a resonant, grave, melodious voice; occasional nasality or sing-song; sudden pauses and resumptions; powerful gestures (e.g., striking off his hat); extempore delivery leaving few verbatim records. The account stresses 'magnetism' or rapport beyond learned art, and compares Hicks's effect to that of other passionate preachers (e.g., Father Taylor). Emotional impact (many in tears) is a key sign of effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preaching venues / accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Preaches anywhere—no respect to buildings: private or public houses, school-rooms, barns, even theatres or ball-rooms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful itinerant minister will make use of any available space to reach audiences, from humble to genteel settings; the venue can be strikingly incongruous (e.g., a ball-room used for concerts). The text uses venue variety to illustrate accessibility and universality of message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine: primacy of the 'inward light' / inward law
rubrics_metrics.description: All true and saving knowledge of God comes from an inward law and light; that inward light is the rule by which people are justified or condemned, not external creeds or literal texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inward light is described as the indelible law written on every heart; scriptures and books cannot supply what the inward light does. The page presents this as both theological principle and practical ethical standard (binding people in love, leading to peace and the end of wars when universally heeded).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive principle: spiritual (not literal) reading of scripture
rubrics_metrics.description: Biblical texts and prophecies are to be taken in their spiritual meaning rather than literal sense; the language of prophecy alludes to spiritual exaltation and moral transformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay gives instances where prophetic imagery (e.g., swords into ploughshares, wolf with lamb) should be read spiritually as moral/exalted states rather than materially literal events. This interpretive stance supports the inward-light doctrine and underpins Hicks's preaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral epistemology: inward conscience over external authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideals of character, justice, and religious action are to follow the inward, Deity-planted law of the emotional soul, not outside doctrines, creeds, legislative enactments, conventionalities, or even decorums.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion frames moral judgment as internal and intuitive; it explains Hicks's emphasis on conscience and why Quaker practice can reject established external authorities. The essay notes that rigidly carrying this out can sometimes produce unseemly or extreme acts in historical records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wartime conduct and neutrality for Friends
rubrics_metrics.description: During war Friends must steer between patriotic convictions and non-warring pledges by not meddling in the controversy and by preserving access to meetings on both sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical practice cited: Friends, by maintaining neutrality, were allowed passage through both armies and could hold yearly meetings. However, practical dilemmas arose (e.g., accepting rent from occupying troops for storage of military stores) and were subject to collective judgment (returning money, referrals to higher meetings). The standard emphasizes practical neutrality and careful adjudication of actions that might conflict with pacifist principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preaching content: moral appeal rather than doctrinal controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer pleading, tender, moral, nearly agonizing conviction that appeals to the inner light rather than engaging in doctrinal disputes or sectarian argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes Hicks typically avoided alluding to internal Quaker disputes and instead delivered appeals to conscience and love that moved diverse audiences. Effectiveness is measured by sympathetic response and inward conviction rather than winning theological debates.
